text: Time to put the last four lessons together. In this lab you'll build state vectors, apply gates, find eigenvalues, combine systems with Kronecker products, and finish with the single most important sanity check in quantum computing: confirming a matrix is actually unitary.

Five tasks, in order. Build and normalize a state vector, and confirm its probabilities sum to exactly one. Apply a gate and check the result against a known eigenvector, using np dot allclose rather than a plain equality check. Combine two single-qubit states with np dot kron into one 4-dimensional two-qubit state. And the capstone check: confirm U at-sign U dot conj dot T equals the identity matrix, the condition that guarantees a gate preserves total probability.

Pauli-X applied to the plus state should leave it unchanged, since plus is X's eigenvector with eigenvalue positive one. The computed result, point seven zero seven one, point seven zero seven one, is identical to plus itself. Notice the use of np dot allclose instead of a plain equals sign — floating-point results can differ by a tiny rounding amount, so allclose checks close enough within tolerance instead, which is the correct real-world habit.

Hadamard was real, so that unitarity check was almost too easy. Pauli-Y has genuinely imaginary entries, a better test of whether conj actually matters. Y dot conj dot T turns out to equal Y itself, since Y is Hermitian, and Y at-sign Y dot conj dot T computes to exactly the identity matrix, confirming Pauli-Y is a physically valid quantum gate despite its complex entries.
Chapter 3 moves into complex numbers themselves: the arithmetic every quantum amplitude actually depends on, and the unitary and Hermitian checks you just ran here, applied more generally.
